claim: ATP is a ubiquitous extracellular signaling messenger.
source: Adenosine 5' triphosphate (ATP) is a ubiquitous extracellular signaling messenger.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about ATP's role.

claim: The Cy3-labeled glutamine-105 mutant (Q105C-Cy3; designated ATPOS) shows a large fluorescence change in the presence of ATP.
source: Screening revealed that the Cy3-labeled glutamine-105 mutant (Q105C-Cy3; designated ATPOS) shows a large fluorescence change in the presence of ATP, with submicromolar affinity, pH-independence, and high selectivity for ATP over ATP metabolites and other nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from the screening described in the manuscript.

claim: ATPOS has submicromolar affinity for ATP.
source: Screening revealed that the Cy3-labeled glutamine-105 mutant (Q105C-Cy3; designated ATPOS) shows a large fluorescence change in the presence of ATP, with submicromolar affinity, pH-independence, and high selectivity for ATP over ATP metabolites and other nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from characterization of ATPOS.

claim: ATPOS shows pH-independence.
source: Screening revealed that the Cy3-labeled glutamine-105 mutant (Q105C-Cy3; designated ATPOS) shows a large fluorescence change in the presence of ATP, with submicromolar affinity, pH-independence, and high selectivity for ATP over ATP metabolites and other nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from characterization of ATPOS.

claim: ATPOS shows high selectivity for ATP over ATP metabolites and other nucleotides.
source: Screening revealed that the Cy3-labeled glutamine-105 mutant (Q105C-Cy3; designated ATPOS) shows a large fluorescence change in the presence of ATP, with submicromolar affinity, pH-independence, and high selectivity for ATP over ATP metabolites and other nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding from characterization of ATPOS.

claim: ATPOS complex binds to neurons in cerebral cortex of living mice.
source: The resulting ATPOS complex binds to neurons in cerebral cortex of living mice, and clearly visualized a concentrically propagating wave of extracellular ATP release in response to electrical stimulation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from in vivo experiments.

claim: ATPOS clearly visualized a concentrically propagating wave of extracellular ATP release in response to electrical stimulation.
source: The resulting ATPOS complex binds to neurons in cerebral cortex of living mice, and clearly visualized a concentrically propagating wave of extracellular ATP release in response to electrical stimulation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from in vivo experiments.

claim: ATP plays important roles as an extracellular signaling molecule in neurotransmission.
source: Adenosine 5' triphosphate (ATP) is the essential energy currency of intracellular metabolism of all living systems, but also plays important roles as an extracellular signaling molecule in a wide variety of physiological and pathological processes, including neurotransmission (Burnstock, 2007), neuron–glia signaling (Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Khakh and North, 2012), tissue circulation (Cheng et al., 2018; González-Alonso et al., 2002; MacVicar and Newman, 2015), regulation of the immune system (Idzko et al., 2014; Junger, 2011), and cancer development (Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Stagg and Smyth, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burnstock, 2007.

claim: ATP plays important roles as an extracellular signaling molecule in neuron-glia signaling.
source: Adenosine 5' triphosphate (ATP) is the essential energy currency of intracellular metabolism of all living systems, but also plays important roles as an extracellular signaling molecule in a wide variety of physiological and pathological processes, including neurotransmission (Burnstock, 2007), neuron–glia signaling (Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Khakh and North, 2012), tissue circulation (Cheng et al., 2018; González-Alonso et al., 2002; MacVicar and Newman, 2015), regulation of the immune system (Idzko et al., 2014; Junger, 2011), and cancer development (Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Stagg and Smyth, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Khakh and North, 2012.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2018; González-Alonso et al., 2002; MacVicar and Newman, 2015.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Idzko et al., 2014; Junger, 2011.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Stagg and Smyth, 2010.

claim: Bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase have been developed for measurement of ATP.
source: To date, a variety of techniques for measurement of ATP have been developed: bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase (Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000), electrochemical methods including voltammetry (Singhal and Kuhr, 1997), enzyme-coupled electrode techniques (Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005), cell-based electrophysiological techniques (Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007), and whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator (Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000.

claim: Electrochemical methods including voltammetry have been developed for measurement of ATP.
source: To date, a variety of techniques for measurement of ATP have been developed: bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase (Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000), electrochemical methods including voltammetry (Singhal and Kuhr, 1997), enzyme-coupled electrode techniques (Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005), cell-based electrophysiological techniques (Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007), and whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator (Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singhal and Kuhr, 1997.

claim: Enzyme-coupled electrode techniques have been developed for measurement of ATP.
source: To date, a variety of techniques for measurement of ATP have been developed: bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase (Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000), electrochemical methods including voltammetry (Singhal and Kuhr, 1997), enzyme-coupled electrode techniques (Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005), cell-based electrophysiological techniques (Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007), and whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator (Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005.

claim: Cell-based electrophysiological techniques have been developed for measurement of ATP.
source: To date, a variety of techniques for measurement of ATP have been developed: bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase (Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000), electrochemical methods including voltammetry (Singhal and Kuhr, 1997), enzyme-coupled electrode techniques (Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005), cell-based electrophysiological techniques (Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007), and whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator (Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007.

claim: Whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator have been developed for measurement of ATP.
source: To date, a variety of techniques for measurement of ATP have been developed: bioluminescence assay methods using firefly luciferase (Holton, 1959; Pellegatti et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2000), electrochemical methods including voltammetry (Singhal and Kuhr, 1997), enzyme-coupled electrode techniques (Kueng et al., 2004; Llaudet et al., 2005), cell-based electrophysiological techniques (Brown and Dale, 2002; Pangrsic et al., 2007), and whole cell-based fluorescence assay methods using Ca2+ indicator (Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anselmi et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2007.

claim: Some ATP measurement techniques have been applied to measure extracellular ATP concentrations in vivo.
source: Some of them have been applied to measure extracellular ATP concentrations in vivo (Gourine et al., 2005; Melani et al., 2005; Pellegatti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gourine et al., 2005; Melani et al., 2005; Pellegatti et al., 2008.

claim: Bioluminescence assay is able to quantify the extracellular ATP levels in microdialysis samples.
source: For example, bioluminescence assay is able to quantify the extracellular ATP levels in microdialysis samples (Melani et al., 2005), and enzyme-coated electrodes inserted in tissues allow continuous monitoring of extracellular ATP levels in the brain (Gourine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Melani et al., 2005.

claim: Enzyme-coated electrodes inserted in tissues allow continuous monitoring of extracellular ATP levels in the brain.
source: For example, bioluminescence assay is able to quantify the extracellular ATP levels in microdialysis samples (Melani et al., 2005), and enzyme-coated electrodes inserted in tissues allow continuous monitoring of extracellular ATP levels in the brain (Gourine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gourine et al., 2005.

claim: Bioluminescence and enzyme-coated electrode methods do not provide spatial information.
source: However, these methods do not provide spatial information.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the methods described in the previous sentence.

claim: Engineered cells displaying luciferase on the plasma membrane were used to visualize extracellular ATP in vivo by inoculating the cells into living mice.
source: Imaging of the bioluminescence generated by luciferin-luciferase reaction might be a solution for spatially resolved measurement of ATP (Rajendran et al., 2016), and indeed, engineered cells displaying luciferase on the plasma membrane were used to visualize extracellular ATP in vivo by inoculating the cells into living mice (Pellegatti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pellegatti et al., 2008.

claim: Both spatial resolution and temporal resolution in luciferase-based imaging are inherently compromised by the low photon flux of bioluminescence emission.
source: However, both spatial resolution and temporal resolution in luciferase-based imaging are inherently compromised by the low photon flux of bioluminescence emission (Rajendran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rajendran et al., 2016.

claim: Imaging techniques using fluorescent sensors can provide excellent spatiotemporal resolution.
source: On the other hand, imaging techniques using fluorescent sensors can provide excellent spatiotemporal resolution (Giepmans et al., 2006), and a variety of fluorescent ATP sensors based on fluorescent proteins have been developed (Arai et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2009; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Tantama et al., 2013; Yaginuma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Giepmans et al., 2006.

claim: A variety of fluorescent ATP sensors based on fluorescent proteins have been developed.
source: On the other hand, imaging techniques using fluorescent sensors can provide excellent spatiotemporal resolution (Giepmans et al., 2006), and a variety of fluorescent ATP sensors based on fluorescent proteins have been developed (Arai et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2009; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Tantama et al., 2013; Yaginuma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arai et al., 2018; Berg et al., 2009; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Tantama et al., 2013; Yaginuma et al., 2015.

claim: Genetically encoded ATP sensors can visualize intracellular ATP dynamics.
source: These genetically encoded ATP sensors can visualize intracellular ATP dynamics, and have facilitated our understanding of ATP signaling inside cells (Depaoli et al., 2018; Zala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Depaoli et al., 2018; Zala et al., 2013.

claim: In vivo imaging of extracellular ATP is still difficult.
source: In contrast, attempts to adapt the existing sensors for extracellular use have achieved limited success, and in vivo imaging of extracellular ATP is still difficult (Conley et al., 2017; Lobas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conley et al., 2017; Lobas et al., 2019.

claim: The affinities of extracellular ATP sensors are too low to monitor extracellular ATP.
source: One problem is that the affinities of these extracellular ATP sensors are too low to monitor extracellular ATP, the concentration of which likely ranges from hundreds of nanomolar to micromolar levels (Yegutkin, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a problem with existing sensors, with citation to Yegutkin, 2008 for the concentration range.

claim: Extracellular ATP concentration likely ranges from hundreds of nanomolar to micromolar levels.
source: One problem is that the affinities of these extracellular ATP sensors are too low to monitor extracellular ATP, the concentration of which likely ranges from hundreds of nanomolar to micromolar levels (Yegutkin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yegutkin, 2008.

claim: Imperfect membrane transport can compromise the performance of extracellular ATP sensors.
source: Moreover, these extracellular ATP sensors are designed to be synthesized inside the cells and transported to the plasma membrane to face the extracellular space (Conley et al., 2017; Lobas et al., 2019). Imperfect membrane transport as well as potential posttranslational modifications such as glycosylation during this process can compromise the performance of the sensors (Morciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morciano et al., 2017.

claim: Potential posttranslational modifications such as glycosylation can compromise the performance of extracellular ATP sensors.
source: Moreover, these extracellular ATP sensors are designed to be synthesized inside the cells and transported to the plasma membrane to face the extracellular space (Conley et al., 2017; Lobas et al., 2019). Imperfect membrane transport as well as potential posttranslational modifications such as glycosylation during this process can compromise the performance of the sensors (Morciano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morciano et al., 2017.

claim: Genetically encoded ATP sensors show strong pH dependency due to the innate pH sensitivity of the fluorescent proteins used.
source: Another problem is the strong pH dependency of these genetically encoded ATP sensors, due to the innate pH sensitivity of the fluorescent proteins used (Chudakov et al., 2010; Tsien, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chudakov et al., 2010; Tsien, 1998.

claim: Changes in ATP concentration in tissues are often accompanied by pH fluctuations.
source: This pH dependence is especially problematic in in vivo ATP imaging, because changes in ATP concentration in tissues are often accompanied by pH fluctuations (Berg et al., 2009; Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berg et al., 2009; Di Virgilio et al., 2018; Gourine et al., 2010.

claim: A hybrid-type probe design involves conjugating a small-molecule fluorescent dye to a ligand-binding protein.
source: Another strategy to develop fluorescent sensors is a hybrid-type probe design in which a small-molecule fluorescent dye is conjugated to a ligand-binding protein (Takikawa et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takikawa et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2009.

claim: A hybrid-type glutamate sensor was previously developed in which the AMPA receptor GluR2 subunit is employed as a glutamate-binding protein.
source: We previously developed a hybrid-type glutamate sensor, in which the AMPA receptor GluR2 subunit is employed as a glutamate-binding protein (Namiki et al., 2007), and visualized extrasynaptic glutamate dynamics in vivo (Okubo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Namiki et al., 2007.

claim: Extrasynaptic glutamate dynamics were visualized in vivo using a hybrid-type glutamate sensor.
source: We previously developed a hybrid-type glutamate sensor, in which the AMPA receptor GluR2 subunit is employed as a glutamate-binding protein (Namiki et al., 2007), and visualized extrasynaptic glutamate dynamics in vivo (Okubo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okubo et al., 2010.

claim: Bacterial FoF1-ATP synthase ε subunit was adopted as an ATP-binding protein for developing a hybrid-type ATP sensor.
source: In this study, to develop a hybrid-type ATP sensor, we adopted bacterial FoF1-ATP synthase ε subunit as an ATP-binding protein, because fluorescent-dye conjugation has been used to study conformational changes of the protein upon ATP binding (Iino et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for the choice of ATP-binding protein, with citations to Iino et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2007.

claim: Fluorescent-dye conjugation has been used to study conformational changes of FoF1-ATP synthase ε subunit upon ATP binding.
source: In this study, to develop a hybrid-type ATP sensor, we adopted bacterial FoF1-ATP synthase ε subunit as an ATP-binding protein, because fluorescent-dye conjugation has been used to study conformational changes of the protein upon ATP binding (Iino et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iino et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2007.

claim: 134 cysteine mutants covering every position in the amino-acid sequence except for the first position were generated.
source: We generated 134 cysteine mutants covering every position in the amino-acid sequence except for the first position (the initiating methionine).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Four small-molecule fluorescent dyes (Oregon Green, Alexa Fluor 488, Cy3 and SiR650) were used, resulting in the generation of 536 fluorescent conjugates in total.
source: We used four small-molecule fluorescent dyes, Oregon Green (OG), Alexa Fluor 488 (Alexa488), Cy3 and SiR650, resulting in the generation of 536 fluorescent conjugates in total.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: A moderate number of fluorescent conjugates showed detectable fluorescence changes upon application of ATP.
source: For each of the four fluorophores, we found a moderate number of fluorescent conjugates showing detectable fluorescence changes upon application of ATP, but with a large variation in the response (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the screening results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fluorescence response varied depending on the type of fluorophore even if the fluorophore labeling site was the same.
source: Notably, even if the fluorophore labeling site was the same, the fluorescence response varied depending on the type of fluorophore.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the screening results.

claim: In the absence of ATP, ATPOS displayed a fluorescence excitation peak at 556 nm and an emission peak at 566 nm.
source: In the absence of ATP, ATPOS displayed a fluorescence excitation peak at 556 nm and an emission peak at 566 nm (Figure 1C; Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: At 1 mM ATP, ATPOS showed an excitation peak at 556 nm and an emission peak at 564 nm.
source: At 1 mM ATP, the fluorescence intensity of ATPOS increased without any appreciable change in the peak wavelengths (excitation peak at 556 nm, emission peak at 564 nm), while the absorption spectrum showed almost no change upon the addition of ATP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fluorescence quantum yield of ATPOS increased from 0.29 to 0.62 upon addition of 1 mM ATP.
source: On the other hand, the fluorescence quantum yield increased from 0.29 to 0.62 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in Table 1.

claim: The change in fluorescence intensity of ATPOS is due to the change in the quantum yield.
source: The results indicate that the change in fluorescence intensity is due to the change in the quantum yield.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that absorption spectrum showed almost no change while quantum yield increased.

claim: ATPOS has an apparent dissociation constant of ~150 nM for ATP.
source: Fluorescence changes were observed at submicromolar concentrations, and fitting the Hill equation to the dose-response data yielded an apparent dissociation constant of ~150 nM and a Hill coefficient of 1.08.
evidence: This is determined by fitting experimental data to the Hill equation.

claim: ATPOS has a Hill coefficient of 1.08 for ATP binding.
source: Fluorescence changes were observed at submicromolar concentrations, and fitting the Hill equation to the dose-response data yielded an apparent dissociation constant of ~150 nM and a Hill coefficient of 1.08.
evidence: This is determined by fitting experimental data to the Hill equation.

claim: ATPOS binds to ATP with 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: The Hill coefficient value of ~1 suggests that ATPOS binds to ATP with 1:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hill coefficient value of ~1.

claim: The affinity of ATPOS for ATP is about one hundred-fold higher than that for ADP.
source: The affinity for ATP was about one hundred-fold higher than that for ADP, and ATPOS was almost insensitive to other metabolites of ATP, such as AMP and adenosine, and other nucleotides such as GTP, CTP and UTP (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is determined from dose-response curves shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ATPOS is almost insensitive to AMP, adenosine, GTP, CTP and UTP.
source: The affinity for ATP was about one hundred-fold higher than that for ADP, and ATPOS was almost insensitive to other metabolites of ATP, such as AMP and adenosine, and other nucleotides such as GTP, CTP and UTP (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is determined from dose-response curves shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The observed rate constants of ATPOS showed a dose-dependent increase ranging from 5.0 s−1 at 0.5 μM ATP to 8.9 s−1 at 2.0 μM ATP.
source: The observed rate constants showed a dose-dependent increase ranging from 5.0 s−1 at 0.5 μM ATP to 8.9 s−1 at 2.0 μM ATP.
evidence: This is determined from stopped-flow measurements.

claim: The decay rate constant of ATPOS upon a decrease in ATP concentration is 2.0 s−1.
source: We also measured fluorescence decay of ATPOS upon a decrease in ATP concentration, and determined the decay rate constant to be 2.0 s−1.
evidence: This is determined from stopped-flow measurements.

claim: The association and dissociation kinetics of ATPOS is fast enough to monitor ATP dynamics on a time scale of seconds.
source: These results suggest that the association and dissociation kinetics of ATPOS is fast enough to monitor ATP dynamics on a time scale of seconds.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured rate constants.

claim: ATPOS showed no fluorescence response to changes in pH from 6.0 to 8.5 in the presence or absence of ATP.
source: Therefore, we assessed the pH sensitivity of ATPOS and observed no fluorescence response to changes in pH from 6.0 to 8.5 in the presence or absence of ATP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: BoNT/C-Hc is a nontoxic subunit of Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin that binds to the plasma membrane of neurons.
source: Firstly, in order to anchor ATPOS to the outer surface of cell membranes, enabling it to report extracellular ATP in brain tissue, we employed BoNT/C-Hc, a nontoxic subunit of Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin, which binds to the plasma membrane of neurons (Tsukamoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsukamoto et al., 2005.

claim: The ATPOS complex exhibited a large fluorescence change in the red (Cy3) channel and high sensitivity for ATP, comparable to those of ATPOS itself.
source: The ATPOS complex exhibited a large fluorescence change in the red (Cy3) channel and high sensitivity for ATP, comparable to those of ATPOS itself, whereas it showed no fluorescence change in the green (Alexa488) channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATPOS complex showed no fluorescence change in the green (Alexa488) channel.
source: The ATPOS complex exhibited a large fluorescence change in the red (Cy3) channel and high sensitivity for ATP, comparable to those of ATPOS itself, whereas it showed no fluorescence change in the green (Alexa488) channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both red and green fluorescence was observed along the neurons after the ATPOS complex was applied and washed out.
source: After the ATPOS complex was applied, followed by wash-out, both red and green fluorescence was observed along the neurons (Figure 2B), indicating successful anchoring of the ATPOS complex on the neuronal cell surface.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fluorescence intensity in the red channel increased upon ATP addition to neurons labeled with ATPOS complex.
source: The fluorescence intensity in the red channel increased upon ATP addition, but that in the green channel did not; consequently the fluorescence ratio was increased.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from cultured neuron experiments.

claim: The ATPOS complex anchored on the neuronal surface can work as a ratiometric sensor of extracellular ATP.
source: These results indicate that the ATPOS complex anchored on the neuronal surface can work as a ratiometric sensor of extracellular ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that red fluorescence increased while green did not upon ATP addition.

claim: The area labeled by ATPOS gradually spread across the cortex to occupy a region 2 mm in diameter.
source: The area labeled by ATPOS, identified by its fluorescence, gradually spread across the cortex to occupy a region 2 mm in diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fluorescence of ATPOS was stably observed after the end of the injection.
source: The fluorescence of ATPOS was stably observed after the end of the injection.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claim: Blood vessels and cell bodies remained unstained by ATPOS in the cerebral cortex.
source: To examine the distribution of ATPOS in the cerebral cortex with cellular resolution, we performed two-photon imaging of the target cortical area, and found that the blood vessels and cell bodies remained unstained (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ATPOS is immobilized in the extracellular space of the cortex.
source: These results indicate that ATPOS is immobilized in the extracellular space of the cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blood vessels and cell bodies remained unstained.

claim: Injection of ATP elicited an increase of the fluorescence ratio to a peak amplitude of 6.5 ± 0.6% (n = 18 from five mice).
source: Injection of ATP elicited an increase of the fluorescence ratio to a peak amplitude of 6.5 ± 0.6% (n = 18 from five mice) (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In the presence of apyrase, the peak amplitude of the ratio was reduced to 2.4 ± 0.5% (n = 14 from three mice).
source: In the presence of apyrase, the peak amplitude of the ratio was reduced to 2.4 ± 0.5% (n = 14 from three mice), while a sham injection containing bovine serum albumin had almost no effect (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: A sham injection containing bovine serum albumin had almost no effect on the fluorescence response of ATPOS to ATP injection.
source: In the presence of apyrase, the peak amplitude of the ratio was reduced to 2.4 ± 0.5% (n = 14 from three mice), while a sham injection containing bovine serum albumin had almost no effect (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: ATPOS applied in the mouse cortex reports the extracellular ATP concentration.
source: These results support the view that ATPOS applied in the mouse cortex does indeed report the extracellular ATP concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the apyrase experiment showing reduced response.

claim: A propagating wave of neuronal depolarization evoked by electrical stimulation or KCl application to the brain causes elevation of the extracellular ATP concentration.
source: Previous reports indicate that a propagating wave of neuronal depolarization evoked by electrical stimulation or KCl application to the brain (Pietrobon and Moskowitz, 2014) causes elevation of the extracellular ATP concentration (Heinrich et al., 2012; Schock et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pietrobon and Moskowitz, 2014; Heinrich et al., 2012; Schock et al., 2007.

claim: The ratiometric images show a wave-like propagation starting around the electrode upon electrical stimulation.
source: The ratiometric images show a wave-like propagation starting around the electrode (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: A precipitous rise of the fluorescence intensity is seen at the wave front, and the increase shifts in a radial direction away from the stimulation site.
source: A precipitous rise of the fluorescence intensity is seen at the wave front, and the increase shifts in a radial direction away from the stimulation site (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase of the ratio showed a peak amplitude of ~30% and lasted about 2 min.
source: The increase of the ratio, which showed a peak amplitude of ~30%, lasted about 2 min.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claim: In the presence of apyrase, the peak amplitude of the fluorescence response to electrical stimulation was substantially reduced to 15.8 ± 2.5% (n = 7 from five mice) while that of the controls was 31.4 ± 1.4% (n = 11 from five mice).
source: In the presence of apyrase, although a wave-like propagation could still be discerned (Figure 4E and F; Figure 4—video 2), its peak amplitude was substantially reduced to 15.8 ± 2.5% (n = 7 from five mice) while that of the controls was 31.4 ± 1.4% (n = 11 from five mice) (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental measurement shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The wave-like propagation of fluorescence changes of ATPOS reflects the dynamics of extracellular ATP signaling during neuronal excitation.
source: These results suggest that the wave-like propagation of fluorescence changes of ATPOS reflects the dynamics of extracellular ATP signaling during neuronal excitation.
evidence: This is inferred from the apyrase experiment showing reduced response.

claim: ATPOS has very high affinity for ATP with an apparent dissociation constant of ~150 nM.
source: First, ATPOS has a very high affinity for ATP; its apparent dissociation constant is ~150 nM, while those of previously reported fluorescent ATP sensors, such as ATeam, QUEEN and iATPSnFR, are in the range of several micromolar to several millimolar (Arai et al., 2018; Conley et al., 2017; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Yaginuma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of ATPOS, with comparison to other sensors supported by citations.

claim: Previously reported fluorescent ATP sensors such as ATeam, QUEEN and iATPSnFR have dissociation constants in the range of several micromolar to several millimolar.
source: First, ATPOS has a very high affinity for ATP; its apparent dissociation constant is ~150 nM, while those of previously reported fluorescent ATP sensors, such as ATeam, QUEEN and iATPSnFR, are in the range of several micromolar to several millimolar (Arai et al., 2018; Conley et al., 2017; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Yaginuma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arai et al., 2018; Conley et al., 2017; Imamura et al., 2009; Lobas et al., 2019; Yaginuma et al., 2015.

claim: The low affinity of conventional sensors makes them unsuitable for in vivo extracellular ATP imaging.
